docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Scope
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Scope: Judge Brimmer’s Practice Standards (civil), effective December 1, 2025, apply alongside the Federal and Local Rules and the ECF procedures.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Chambers
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Chambers: Don’t contact the law clerks about procedural or scheduling matters. Send a proposed order by email only when chambers asks, as a Word attachment. Don’t submit proposed judgments, since the clerk prepares them. Proposed orders for motions go through CM/ECF.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Extensions and continuances
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Extensions and continuances: An extension needs particular good cause and must be filed no later than three business days before the due date. Agreement of counsel, inconvenience, the press of business, scheduling conflicts, or practicing as a sole practitioner aren’t good cause. Don’t ask for a continuance at the hearing or trial, and a stipulated continuance isn’t effective until the court approves it.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Settlement: Tell his judicial assistant as soon as possible. A hearing or bench trial is vacated only if pleadings that resolve the matter are filed by noon on the last business day before it, or else counsel appear to recite the terms. Jury costs can be assessed under D.C.COLO.LCivR 54.2 if a case settles after noon on the last business day before trial. Settlement talks don’t continue hearings, trials, or deadlines. The court generally won’t retain jurisdiction to enforce a settlement.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Discovery: Deadlines and limits are set by the assigned magistrate judge, and the presumptive discovery period is six months.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Motions: Motions, objections, responses, and briefs are 15 pages and replies 10, including the cover page, statement of facts, and everything but the certificate of service, in 12-point type with footnotes the same size. Summary judgment motions and responses are 20 pages. No surreply without leave, and a motion for leave attaches the proposed surreply. Noncompliant motions may be denied or stricken on the court’s own motion.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Motions to dismiss
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Motions to dismiss: Rule 12(b) motions are discouraged if an amendment can fix the defect, so confer first. Don’t plead a Rule 12(b) motion in the alternative as a Rule 56 motion. For each Rule 12(b)(6) claim, list each element you say wasn’t alleged, and the respondent marks each element “DISPUTED” and cites the page and paragraph where it’s pleaded.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Summary judgment: A numbered Statement of Undisputed Material Facts with specific record cites, a Response, optional Statements of Additional Disputed and Undisputed Facts, and Reply sections, with no legal argument in those sections. Failing to follow this can get the motion struck or facts deemed admitted.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Experts and trial
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Experts and trial: A motion to exclude opinion testimony names each opinion and ground, and the deadline is set at the scheduling conference, otherwise 30 days after rebuttal expert disclosures. Motions in limine are discouraged and are due 14 days before the Trial Preparation Conference, with responses at 7 days. At 14 days before it, file proposed jury instructions with sources, and email them in Word with a separate verdict form. At 7 days, file witness and exhibit lists and voir dire questions. The Trial Preparation Conference is usually about two weeks before trial, and trial counsel must attend in person.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Exhibits and depositions
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Exhibits and depositions: File a joint-style exhibit list on the court’s form two business days before a motion hearing. Plaintiff’s exhibits use yellow labels with numbers and defendant’s use blue labels with letters, bound in labeled notebooks, with separate sets for the court, deputy, reporter, law clerk, opposing counsel, and witness. Designate deposition testimony by page and line, with designations 60 days before trial and counter-designations at 45 days, objections within 14 days in a four-column table.

docs.t: Judge Philip A. Brimmer (D. Colo.) — Jury trials
docs.x: Judge Philip A. Brimmer, D. Colo.. Jury trials: Counsel appear at 8:00 a.m. on the first day and selection starts at 8:30. The jury is usually nine with three peremptory challenges per side and 15 minutes of voir dire per side after the court. Jurors may take notes and receive written instructions, and the jury is charged before closings. The court typically doesn’t sit on Fridays.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Communications
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Communications: Don’t call chambers. Email with the case number and name in the subject and copy all counsel. Chambers can’t give legal advice or grant informal requests not made by motion. Send proposed orders both through CM/ECF and by email in editable Word format, copying all counsel.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Length is by word count
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Length is by word count: Motions, objections, responses, and briefs are limited to 4,000 words, replies to 2,700, and summary judgment and preliminary injunction or restraining order papers to 5,500 words. Footnotes count, and the caption, tables, signature block, and certificates don’t. Every paper must end with a certification, right after the signature block, that it complies with the limit. A motion to exceed the limit is due three business days before the paper is due. Papers by parties without word processing get page limits instead (10, 15, and 20 pages).

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Format and citations
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Format and citations: Any proportionally spaced serif font. Bluebook or any consistent, clear citation form. Give Westlaw cites for unpublished opinions, or attach them. Mark exhibits by number and name, and don’t re-attach exhibits already filed with an earlier paper. No sur-reply or supplemental brief without leave. A notice of supplemental authority may give only the citation, its date, and a one-sentence statement of the issue.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Rule 12 and amendments
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Rule 12 and amendments: Rule 12 motions are discouraged where an amendment can cure the defect, and counsel must confer before any Rule 12(b), (c), (e), or (f) motion and describe the conferral efforts in the motion. Don’t plead a Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion as an alternative Rule 56 motion. The court freely grants a timely motion to amend, and futility arguments are better raised in a Rule 12 motion after the amended pleading is filed.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Summary judgment: A Statement of Undisputed Facts, a Response, a Statement of Additional Facts, and Reply sections, with no legal argument in them. You must admit or deny the factual substance, so you can’t deny based on inadmissibility (object concisely instead), can’t deny for lack of knowledge without a Rule 56(d) request and affidavit, and can’t say a document “speaks for itself.” Failing to follow this can get the motion struck.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Experts and emergencies
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Experts and emergencies: A motion to exclude an expert is due 30 days after rebuttal expert disclosures if the scheduling order has no date, and an issue not raised that way is waived or forfeited. Attach the expert’s full report. An emergency motion is only for imminent, irreparable harm: begin the caption with “Emergency,” use the CM/ECF Emergency event, and email chambers.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Settlement and continuances
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Settlement and continuances: File a notice of settlement stating how long you need for dismissal papers. On the eve of a hearing or trial, also email chambers with “Settlement” in the subject. Nothing is vacated until the court orders it, jury costs can be assessed under Local Civil Rule 54.2 for a settlement after noon on the last business day before a jury trial, and the court generally won’t retain jurisdiction over a settled case. Continuance motions made at the hearing or trial aren’t entertained, and a stipulated continuance isn’t effective until approved.

docs.t: Judge Daniel D. Domenico (D. Colo.) — Courtroom and trial
docs.x: Judge Daniel D. Domenico, D. Colo.. Courtroom and trial: File a glossary five business days before any hearing or trial. Agree on one exhibit numbering system from the start of discovery, use the same numbers for depositions and trial, and mark exhibits by number only. The court sets a Final Pretrial Conference about three to four weeks before trial and a Trial Preparation Conference the week before, and trial counsel must attend both. Make Batson challenges after peremptories end and before the jury is sworn, and ask that jurors not be released. Jurors may take notes and receive written instructions.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Scope and chambers
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Scope and chambers: His Revised Practice Standards (effective December 1, 2022) have the force of orders and add to the Local Rules. Don’t contact chambers about substance. Ex parte contact by letter or phone is barred, so everything goes in a motion, brief, notice, or status report served on all parties. The magistrate judge generally manages discovery and discovery disputes.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Extensions and trial continuances
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Extensions and trial continuances: Seek extensions or continuances by written motion with good cause as far ahead as possible. Absent a compelling reason, an extension motion must be filed by the original deadline and a hearing continuance by the court business day before the hearing. Trial continuances are heavily discouraged and will rarely be granted, and a conflicting trial before another court doesn’t count as substantial good cause.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Motions: One document for motion and argument, with exhibits filed the same day as separate attachments. A proposed order only if chambers asks. Every request for action must be in its own motion, and not in a brief, notice, or response. Tell the court if a motion becomes moot. Page limits are 15 for most motions and responses with 10 for replies, 10 for Rule 702 motions with a 5-page reply, 10 for Rule 72 objections and responses, and 30 pages with a 15-page reply for a traditional summary judgment motion. No sur-reply or supplemental brief without leave. Oral argument is at his sole discretion, with a preference when an attorney with eight years or less experience will argue.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Rule 12 and amendments
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Rule 12 and amendments: He views Rule 12 motions as overused. Counsel must confer first, even though the local rule says otherwise, and the motion must have a conspicuous statement of the efforts made, or the movant risks a personal fee award. Defending a Rule 12(b)(6) motion with facts outside the complaint violates his standards. All Rule 12 requests go in one motion that names the subsection. A motion to amend attaches a clean copy and a redline.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Summary judgment: Each party gets one summary judgment motion, plus one optional Early Motion for Partial Summary Judgment filed within 30 days of the initial scheduling order. A Movant’s Statement of Material Facts, a Response to it, a Statement of Additional Disputed Facts, and Reply sections follow the same restrictions as other D. Colo. judges: no denial for inadmissibility, no denial for lack of knowledge without a Rule 56(d) request and affidavit, no “speaks for itself.”

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Motions in limine and experts
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Motions in limine and experts: Each side gets one motion in limine, 10 pages with a 5-page response and no reply, after conferral, filed no earlier than 70 days and no later than 21 days before the Final Trial Preparation Conference. A Rule 702 motion is due 70 days before that conference, or with the summary judgment response or reply if it targets summary judgment evidence, and must not be styled a motion in limine.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Pretrial: The magistrate judge holds the Final Pretrial Conference, and he holds a Final Trial Preparation Conference about two weeks before a civil trial, which trial counsel must attend in person or risk sanctions. Seven days before it, file the Final Witness List (listing will-call and may-call witnesses with time estimates), a Final List of Proposed Exhibits (no duplicates, with stipulations marked), proposed voir dire, and a list of open issues. Jury instructions, the statement of the case, and verdict forms are due 14 days before. Ask for a trial longer than five days within three days after the Final Pretrial Order.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Settlement: He won’t vacate the trial preparation conference or trial until you file a stipulation of dismissal or a stipulated notice of settlement saying all material terms are agreed. If court approval is needed, he won’t vacate until a motion for preliminary approval is filed. Within one week of scheduling a settlement conference or mediation, file a notice of it, and within three court days afterward file a notice of the outcome.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Trial and exhibits
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Trial and exhibits: Trial days start at 8:45 a.m. with counsel present at 8:30. Openings are 20 minutes per side, sidebars are discouraged, and leading questions on direct are readily sustained. Plaintiff’s exhibits are numbers and defendant’s are letters, with no duplicates, original binders for witnesses, copies for the court, and flash drives for the reporter. Designate depositions 21 days before trial, and file a joint marked transcript of objections seven days before. Don’t use deposition testimony of a witness who testifies live, except as the rules allow. Civil juries are eight with three peremptory strikes each, and Batson challenges come after strikes and before the jury is sworn.

docs.t: Judge William J. Martínez (D. Colo.) — Special matters
docs.x: Judge William J. Martínez, D. Colo.. Special matters: Don’t expect a TRO to issue ex parte except in strict compliance with Rule 65(b). A pending TRO or preliminary injunction motion refiled after removal will likely be stricken without prejudice. The Initial Discovery Protocols apply in employment cases alleging adverse action, within 30 days after the defendant’s first response.

docs.t: Judge Raymond P. Moore (D. Colo.) — Where they are
docs.x: Judge Raymond P. Moore, D. Colo.. Where they are: He posts civil Practice Standards, and the version we found is dated May 2013. They cover courtroom procedure, a required exhibit list and witness list form, and a Rule 56.1 summary judgment procedure. We haven’t read the details.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Scope
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Scope: Her Individual Rules and Practices (revised April 2020) control over any conflict with the Local Rules. Motions that don’t follow them are summarily denied. The motion rules don’t apply to Social Security appeals, habeas cases, bankruptcy appeals, pro se prisoner civil rights cases, or student loan cases.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions: Ask in writing at least 48 hours before the date. State the original date, how many prior requests and how they were ruled on, and whether the other side consents and, if not, why. If other dates are affected, attach a proposed scheduling order that uses only business days.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Pre-motion letter and conference
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Pre-motion letter and conference: Before a motion to dismiss, for judgment on the pleadings, for summary judgment, for preliminary injunctive relief, or for sanctions, send a letter of no more than three double-spaced pages stating the grounds. The other side answers within three business days in three pages, describing its arguments and defenses. Don’t file the motion until the court enters an order on the letters. A Rule 12(b) letter stays the time to answer or move. Motions to dismiss are decided with prejudice unless the opposing party amended as of right before the motion or files, and the court grants, a cross-motion to amend.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Orders to show cause
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Orders to show cause: Any application by order to show cause needs a written explanation, with authority, of why ordinary motion practice isn’t available.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Briefs
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Briefs: Memoranda are up to 25 double-spaced pages and replies 10, with a table of contents and a table of authorities for any over 10 pages. One-inch margins and 12-point type for text and footnotes. Several parties on one side file jointly unless the court allows otherwise, and all opposing parties file one joint opposition, with any cross-motion inside it. One reply per motion, covering the cross-motion. No sur-reply without permission, requested by a one-page letter.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Filing
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Filing: Each exhibit is a separate docket attachment labeled with its number and a short description. Courtesy copies only when ordered, printed from CM/ECF, and bound, tabbed, and indexed. Most motions are decided on submission. Nothing may be filed under seal without prior authorization, with a declaration showing good cause and a proposed confidentiality order containing the language she specifies. A motion for default judgment needs a certificate of service showing it was served on the defaulting party.

docs.t: Judge Mae D’Agostino (N.D.N.Y.) — Removed cases
docs.x: Judge Mae D’Agostino, N.D.N.Y.. Removed cases: Within seven days after filing a notice of removal, file and serve a signed statement giving each defendant’s date of receiving and of service of the summons and complaint, New York citizenship for diversity cases (with each member’s citizenship for entities), reasons if removal came more than 30 days after the first receipt, and any served defendant who didn’t join and why.

docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Dispositive motions: He requires a request for a pre-filing conference before any motion to dismiss or for summary judgment. For a motion to dismiss, ask as soon as possible after service of the summons and complaint. For summary judgment, ask usually no later than 45 days before the discovery deadline in the case management plan.

docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and schedule
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and schedule: He treats the Rule 26(f) report as one of the most important filings and wants a firm, realistic discovery completion date, since all other dates run from it. A settlement conference is usually within 30 days after discovery closes, the joint trial memorandum is usually due 60 days after that, and the case goes on the jury list for the following month. Extensions are granted for good cause, but he’s concerned by repeated requests to move the discovery deadline.

docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Motions practice
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Motions practice: Discovery motions usually go to a magistrate judge, and he usually doesn’t refer dispositive motions. He likes chambers’ copies of dispositive motions. He feels strongly against letter briefs, even to cite new authority: file a request for leave to file a supplemental brief with the brief attached. He has no set policy on sur-replies or reconsideration motions. Lawyer affidavits shouldn’t be filed unless needed to prove something within the lawyer’s exclusive knowledge. He won’t grant ex parte TRO relief without extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Conferences and settlement
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Conferences and settlement: He often holds pretrial conferences by telephone. He usually doesn’t take part in settlement conferences, relying on magistrate judges, para-judicial officers, and special masters.

docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Trial: Trials run Monday through Thursday, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Attach motions in limine to the joint trial memorandum, and they are decided at the final pretrial conference. Exhibits approved at that conference are pre-marked and in evidence. He asks the submitted voir dire questions and lets counsel follow up. Civil juries are eight with no alternates, juror notes are allowed, and the charge is given in writing. He grants a request for a concise, non-argumentative opening and usually gives one hour for closing with 15 minutes of rebuttal. No arguments in front of the jury, and raise procedural issues before or after the trial day or at breaks.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Discovery disputes: He tries to resolve discovery disputes by brief letters or a conference call and doesn’t allow discovery motions or briefs before the call. Follow his Instructions on Discovery Disputes. He decides most discovery disputes himself, and counsel must take part in conference calls, often on short notice. Don’t call chambers ex parte except to ask for a settlement conference, and have all parties on the line.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Motions: No sur-replies and no letter briefs: file a formal motion, and for new authority file a notice of supplemental authority. He has no individual rules on dispositive motions apart from valuing brevity, and pre-filing conferences aren’t required unless he orders one. For an urgent motion, file it and send chambers a copy with a short cover letter. No response to a motion for reconsideration unless he allows it, usually with the full 21 days from his order. Motions to extend time follow Local Rule 7(b).

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: The next business day after e-filing, deliver one bound paper copy to the clerk’s office, printed from the docket with the ECF header, of TRO, preliminary injunction, and prejudgment remedy papers, summary judgment papers, joint trial memoranda, and trial briefs. Exhibits are separately tabbed. Cite exhibits by their CM/ECF names, and give each a cover sheet.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Argument and scheduling
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Argument and scheduling: He has no motion day and hears argument as his schedule allows, often ruling from the bench even on dispositive motions. He invites junior lawyers to argue and allows a second senior lawyer to argue for the same party. The Rule 26(f) report usually becomes the scheduling order, and he decides whether a scheduling conference is needed. A party seeking a stay of discovery must move for it. Motions for preliminary injunctions get an early telephone conference.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Settlement: He usually refers parties to mediation with a magistrate judge and invites a short joint request. The court won’t retain jurisdiction to enforce a confidential settlement unless the terms are put on the public record with reasons.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Trial: Typical trial days run 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., five days a week. Openings are very short and non-argumentative, and closings are generally 30 minutes. Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged at least seven days before the joint trial memorandum, and unlisted exhibits aren’t admitted absent good cause. Motions in limine are due 30 days before the first pretrial conference. Civil juries are at least eight and usually nine, with note-taking, and he charges the jury before closings. No re-cross, and sidebars are rare.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: He doesn’t routinely hear argument but will ask for it if it would clarify an issue, and he considers requests after reading the papers. He may tell counsel beforehand which issues interest him. He rules from the bench on an ad hoc basis.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and conferences
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and conferences: He uses the report to spot inefficiencies and routinely schedules a telephone conference. He usually reads new complaints before the report comes in, to check for conflicts and issues that might need his attention. He may use pre-argument conferences on dispositive motions, for example to get an amended complaint instead of a ruling on a motion to dismiss, or to simplify a complaint when a motion to amend is filed.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Briefs and affidavits
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Briefs and affidavits: File a motion for permission, stating the basis, before a sur-reply. He discourages letter briefs. To raise new case law, file a request for leave to file a supplemental brief with the brief and the cases attached. He doesn’t favor lawyer affidavits, since he treats all statements by counsel as representations to the court. He reads reconsideration motions carefully for whether they meet the procedural requirements.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies and extensions
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies and extensions: He prefers chambers’ copies, and the requirements are in the electronic filing order entered on the docket in each case. He usually grants extensions unless good cause is missing or the privilege has been abused.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Discovery and settlement
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Discovery and settlement: He frequently but not always refers discovery motions to a magistrate judge and usually tries to resolve the rest by conference call. He prefers not to hold settlement conferences himself and refers them to a magistrate judge or a para-judicial officer.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Emergency relief: Before acting on a TRO motion he usually seeks the defendant’s input. He has no set procedure for preliminary injunctions but often asks if the parties will consolidate the hearing with the final hearing. He typically refers prejudgment-remedy motions to a magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Joint trial memorandum and motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Joint trial memorandum and motions in limine: Dispose of all motions before you file the joint trial memorandum, and file any motions in limine with it. He wants Daubert and other motions in limine raised in advance, preferably by the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Trial: He generally starts between 9:30 and 10:00 a.m. and runs to 4:30 or 5:00, with two 15-minute breaks and a 45-minute to one-hour lunch, five days a week, and he starts on time. He doesn’t usually limit trial or witness time, but may split the time if estimates look excessive. He suggests ten minutes per side for openings and sets closings with counsel, from half an hour to an hour and a half. Objections during closing may be sustained. At the final pretrial conference he asks what demonstratives you have and whether you want court equipment to show them. He generally doesn’t admit them as full exhibits but allows marking for identification, and encourages exchanging them early. Stipulate to as many exhibits as possible. Pre-mark all exhibits and submit them to him in binders at least three days before trial. The pre-marked numbers are the trial nu

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and schedule
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and schedule: He treats the Rule 26(f) report as critical, and his courtroom deputy sends a notice if it is late. Every proposed date must fall on a Friday. The report must show you consulted your clients (and known witnesses if needed), give a meaningful overview including whether claims can be narrowed and whether settlement talks would help now, and use realistic dates built for the case. Beyond Form 26(f), add a Subsection V.E.1 with a date for a post-discovery telephone status conference, no earlier than two weeks after discovery closes and before the dispositive-motion deadline. If dispositive motions are filed, the joint trial memorandum is due within 30 days of the ruling and the case is trial-ready 30 days after that. If none are filed, the memorandum is due 45 days after discovery closes and trial-ready 45 days after the memor

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Motions and argument
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Motions and argument: He hears argument on dispositive motions to address questions counsel can resolve in person, and on non-dispositive motions only when it will materially advance the case. He may rule from the bench. Sur-replies are rarely needed: file a motion for permission with the brief. Don’t file letter briefs unless he asks; file a formal motion instead, and use a notice of supplemental authority for new cases. For urgent motions, file with the Clerk and send chambers a copy with a short cover letter explaining the urgency. Attorney affidavits aren’t needed to identify exhibits or deposition transcripts on dispositive motions, and he rarely accepts them as evidence on disputed facts other than attorneys’ fees.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Extensions: He is likely to grant an extension when all parties consent and it doesn’t affect the scheduling order. Otherwise Local Rule 7(b) good cause applies. He asks that, absent extraordinary or supervening circumstances, you file at least seven calendar days before the date at issue.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Discovery disputes: Don’t file a discovery motion until you have discussed the dispute with him. File a joint motion for a discovery conference that describes the dispute, says you conferred in good faith, lists the issues, and gives dates and times you’re available for a telephone conference. At least a week before the conference, each side files a brief of no more than 5 pages. He decides most disputes himself and may refer others to a randomly assigned magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief and copies
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Emergency relief and copies: No ex parte TRO without extraordinary circumstances, and he usually asks the lawyer to try to reach the other side by phone. Preliminary-injunction motions get an early telephone conference to see if discovery is needed and to encourage combining the hearing with a trial on the merits. Chambers’ courtesy copies of e-filed documents are not required.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Trial: Typical days run 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with an hour for lunch and two 15-minute breaks, five days a week. Long cases may run 9:00 to 5:00 four days a week. He usually sets no time limits, but his pretrial order requires you to separate witnesses and exhibits you “intend” to call or use from those you “may.” Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged under that order, with one set for him and one for his clerk. Openings in civil cases must be non-argumentative and usually run ten minutes or less; closings are generally 30 minutes. Disclose demonstratives before use; they can’t be used in closing unless marked as an exhibit or shared with the others at least a day earlier. File motions in limine with or before the joint trial memorandum. State objections in a few words with no argument; he rarely allows sidebars. Submit proposed jury instructions with t

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Criminal cases: He is paired with Magistrate Judge Garfinkel for initial presentments, where a scheduling order with a jury selection date issues. Pleas are before him; call the number on his page to schedule one. A continuance motion that touches the Speedy Trial Act gets a telephone status conference and must come with a signed waiver from each defendant. In cases with identifiable victims, the prosecutor must email the chambers law clerk at least 24 hours before any public proceeding to certify compliance with the Crime Victims’ Rights Act.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: He hears argument on dispositive motions when, after reading the papers, he still has questions counsel can resolve, and rarely grants one without letting counsel argue. He hears non-dispositive motions only when argument will materially advance the case. He often schedules dispositive motions for a motion day and rules from the bench, even on dispositive motions.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and conferences
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and conferences: If your deadlines are reasonable, the report becomes the initial scheduling order. It should give a meaningful overview and help the parties consider narrowing claims and settlement. He generally honors requests for status or settlement conferences. Conference calls can replace most chambers conferences, and he requires counsel to join calls, often on short notice, when a prompt call will help. He encourages you to contact chambers when discovery disputes arise.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Briefs
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Briefs: Sur-replies are rarely necessary, but he generally grants a motion for leave. He occasionally asks for letter briefs, which are docketed as pleadings. Otherwise briefs must follow the Local Rules. Reconsideration motions must follow Local Rule 7(c). Lawyer affidavits may be used to identify exhibits and transcripts on dispositive motions, but are rarely if ever accepted as evidence on disputed facts other than attorneys’ fees.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies and extensions
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies and extensions: He appreciates copies of dispositive and emergency motions and trial memoranda, including requests to charge. Don’t send other filings. Print from the docket with the ECF header, use a three-ring binder if a staple won’t hold, and tab each exhibit separately. Double-sided is fine. Reasonable extension requests are generally granted. Negotiate one all parties accept and say it is on consent. State the reason and the number of earlier extensions.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Discovery and referrals
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Discovery and referrals: He prefers to resolve discovery disputes by conference call and decides most himself, referring a few to a magistrate judge. He doesn’t refer all motions of any one type, and referrals depend on each judge’s involvement and time and can be sent back. Even after briefing, he expects the parties to keep trying to resolve it, and costs may be awarded under Rule 37(a)(5) when the court has to step in.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Emergency relief: He is extremely reluctant to grant ex parte TROs and requires strict compliance with Rule 65. TRO and preliminary-injunction hearings are normally set by order to show cause, and when possible after a conference with all counsel. Put the precise relief you want in a draft order, and support it with a memorandum and non-attorney affidavits.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Settlement and joint trial memoranda
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Settlement and joint trial memoranda: His status report orders require the parties to certify they discussed settlement in good faith since the order. He schedules a settlement conference on request or when it looks useful, usually with a magistrate judge or the special masters program. He encourages a settlement conference before you spend on the joint trial memorandum. The pretrial order calling for it issues after the dispositive-motion deadline, and a joint motion can postpone it if serious settlement talks are underway. His order is similar to, but not the same as, the standing order on trial memoranda. Send chambers a courtesy copy, including proposed findings or requests to charge. When the memorandum is ordered, the case goes on a trial calendar, and at the calendar call counsel report on the availability of parties and witnesses and jury sele

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Trial: Lawyers report at 9:00 a.m. and the jury sits from about 9:30 to 5:00, five days a week. He keeps lawyers after 5:00 for objections. He sets no time limits but presses you to lower unreasonable estimates. His pretrial order requires separating witnesses and exhibits you “intend” to call or use from those you “may,” telling the other side the order of witnesses in advance, and exchanging pre-marked exhibits, with one set for him and one for his clerk. He encourages affidavits or color-coded deposition transcripts in place of direct testimony in bench trials and urgent matters when counsel agree. He routinely sequesters non-party and non-expert witnesses, even without a motion. docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Communicating with chambers

docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery: The report should give a meaningful overview and usually becomes the scheduling order.
